name: Platinum Grey
lede: Platinum Grey is a near-neutral medium grey taken from RAL 7036, named for the pale metal platinum rather than any platinum-based pigment.

sections.title: A metal's name, not its pigment
sections.body:
Our library lists Platinum Grey as RAL 7036 [1]. RAL, the German industrial color standard, began in 1927 with a first set of forty swatches, RAL 840, issued so that paint could be specified by number instead of by physical sample [2]. Platinum, the metal, is itself a near-white, slightly grey metal, and the name here borrows that association rather than describing any pigment made from it: no platinum compound is a common artist's or industrial colorant [1][2].

In Munsell terms the library records this grey as N 6.1, a pure neutral with almost no color cast (LCH chroma just 1.7) [1]. That puts it a step darker than [[silver|Silver]] and close to [[irisglow|Irisglow]] and [[plumbago-grey|Plumbago Grey]] in our data, though all are simply shades of neutral grey [1]. Beyond the RAL code, no further naming history is documented here [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A screen match for this grey appears in 921 of 23,781 paintings, about 3.9 percent, as photographed, with its highest coverage in Christen Købke's 1831 cloud study *Studie af skyer*, where it fills most of the canvas [1]. It is nearly two and a half times more common in paintings from the 1900s than the archive average, often in skies, stone and fabric rather than skin [1]. The match is computed from photographs of aged, varnished paintings and never identifies a pigment [1].

questions.q: Platinum Grey is named after what?
True or false: Platinum Grey has a noticeable warm or cool color cast.

openers: Platinum Grey borrows a metal's name for its color, though no pigment here is actually made from platinum.

issues: No concordance hits; RAL founding history from one web source, hedged. No documentation found for the specific naming of 7036.
